title: Inside the atom
description: Get to know the tiny pieces that make every element itself.
sourceFiles: Sample course notes — original demonstration content

source.file: Sample course notes — original demonstration content

sections.title: A tiny address book
sections.body: An atom has a small, dense nucleus at its centre and electrons arranged around it. Nearly all of its mass sits in the nucleus; most of the atom is the space around it.

sections.title: Three particles, three jobs
items: Proton: charge +1, relative mass 1; found in the nucleus.
Neutron: charge 0, relative mass 1; found in the nucleus.
Electron: charge −1, relative mass about 1/1836; found outside the nucleus.

sections.title: Atomic number
sections.body: The atomic number (proton number) is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.

sections.title: Identify the element
sections.body: A carbon atom has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6. If it is neutral, it also has 6 electrons. Changing its neutron count would make a different isotope, not a different element.

sections.title: Easy mix-up
sections.body: Electrons are not inside the nucleus. They occupy regions around it and contribute very little to the atom's total mass.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Protons and neutrons form the nucleus. Electrons are outside it. Proton number identifies the element.

sections.title: Same element, different neutron count
sections.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their proton number stays fixed; their mass numbers differ.

sections.title: Read the notation
sections.body:
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = mass number − proton number

sections.title: Carbon dating
sections.body: Carbon-14 used in dating has 6 protons and 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons. It is still carbon because the proton count stays 6; its extra neutrons make it a different isotope.

sections.title: When an atom becomes an ion
sections.body: An ion is a particle with an overall charge because it has gained or lost electrons. The nucleus does not change during ordinary ion formation.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Isotopes differ in neutrons. Ions differ in electrons. Use mass number minus proton number to find neutrons.

sections.title: Electrons occupy shells
sections.body: For the first 20 elements, electrons fill shells from the inside out. The simplified shell capacities used here are 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 8 in the third.

sections.title: Build an arrangement
items: A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons.
Fill the first shell before starting the second.
For elements 1–20, continue 2, 8, 8 before moving outward.

sections.title: Build sodium's shells
sections.body: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons. Fill 2 in the first shell, then 8 in the second; the one left goes in the third: 2, 8, 1.

sections.title: Easy mix-up
sections.body: For a positive ion, subtract electrons; for a negative ion, add electrons. The proton count remains the same.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons. Fill shells from the inside out: 2, then 8, then 8 for the first 20 elements.

questions.prompt: Which particle determines the atomic number of an element?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.prompt: A carbon atom has mass number 14 and proton number 6. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − proton number, so 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.prompt: Two atoms are isotopes of the same element. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.

questions.prompt: A neutral sodium atom has 11 protons. What is its electron arrangement in this simplified model?
questions.explanation: A neutral atom has 11 electrons. Filling shells from the inside gives 2, 8, 1.

questions.prompt: An atom loses one electron. What changes?
questions.explanation: Losing a negatively charged electron leaves the particle with a net positive charge.

questions.prompt: Why does almost all of an atom's mass sit in its nucleus?
options: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus and are much heavier than electrons
The nucleus takes up most of the atom's volume
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons each have relative mass about 1, while an electron is about 1/1836.
